newsitem.title: CHINA: FUND VIEW - South Korea gaining favour.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - South Korea gaining favour.

text.p: Overall sentiment towards South Korea is improving despite a possible downgrade of South Korea's short-term foreign currency ratings by Moody's Investors Service, analysts said.

Moody's on Tuesday said it was reviewing South Korea's short-term foreign currency ratings and long-term foreign currency bank deposit ratings for a possible downgrade, but it affirmed the nation's A-1 foreign currency bond rating.
"A lot of investors accept the fact that Moody's and (Standard & Poor's) are backward-looking agencies," said David Descalzi, senior portfolio manager with Prudential Asia.
"They'll cut their ratings in response to an identified problem and you can't invest on that basis. So from a market basis, I don't think it will have much effect."
In fact, Descalzi said he was becoming more bullish on South Korea, "especially relative to the rest of Asia."
Rising demand in key export markets and a friendlier foreign exchange environment have spurred something of an exports turnaround in South Korea.
"Distant though it seemed just three months ago, a turnaround in Korea's macroeconomic conditions is now becoming very visible," SBC Warburg said recently.
Recent strength of the Japanese yen against the U.S. dollar will assist South Korea, which has devalued its won in a bid to improve competitiveness against Japan in key markets.
South Korea's strong position in high value-added electronics will also help the nation capture the recovery in global demand for electronics products, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG) said recently.

DMG forecasts a 21 percent rise in electronics exports in the second half of 1997 compared with a two percent contraction in the first half this year, while the semiconductor market is expected to grow by 20 percent in the next three years.

Early signs of improvement in both the nation's balance of payments and current account deficit are bound to filter their way through the rest of the economy soon, improving liquidity conditions as the nation's huge conglomerates, or chaebol, struggle to cope with massive debt problems.

But that does not mean the outlook for financial markets is promising in the short term, SBC Warburg said. Although the macro picture appears to be bottoming out, SBC Warburg believes the corporate picture is still not bullish, partly because funding requirements will remain high in the short term.
But Descalzi said opportunities are starting to surface.

"There may be some immediate turbulence because of the excessive debt position of some of these companies," he said. "But the bottom line is you have some very good companies that can earn their way out of the difficulties."
There will be more bankruptcies and restructuring, he said, but there will inevitably be further opening of the capital markets, which will provide longer-term benefits.

"A further opening of the capital markets could be used as an avenue towards restructuring," he said. "A crisis always does concentrate the mind wonderfully and right thinking will move the authorities and the regulators in Korea towards further opening up."
But SBC Warburg cautioned that U.S. dollar-yen fluctuations once again posed the biggest risk to a newly export-competitive South Korea.

An unexpected decline in the yen against the U.S. dollar would destroy its new competitiveness, while a sudden strengthening in the yen against the U.S. dollar would remove any motivation for South Korea to pursue badly needed structural adjustments.
